cards.title: \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) versus \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{BQEXP}\)? In promise-problem terms, does every pair \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of binary strings that has a polynomial-time quantum verifier with two unentangled polynomial-size proofs also admit a uniform quantum algorithm running in time \(2^{p(n)}\), for some polynomial \(p\), with error at most \(1/3\) on every promised input? The algorithm receives no proofs. The polynomial may depend on \(\Pi\) and its verifier, but not on the individual input of length \(n\).
cards.why: Unentangled quantum proofs add a nonconvex constraint to quantum verification. An exponential-time quantum simulation would place a meaningful algorithmic limit on this model and clarify whether its power can be explained without nondeterministic exponential-time witness search.
cards.status_note: The source explicitly asks this inclusion in January 2026. Primary definitions and the NEXP upper bound were checked together with July 2026 hierarchy and stoquastic results on 2026-09-14. None of those checked results supplies a BQEXP simulation for general QMA(2); this is a bounded literature check.

progress.text: Harrow and Montanaro establish amplification and compression to two unentangled proofs and describe the standard NEXP upper bound.
The source problem list explicitly asks for containment in bounded-error quantum exponential time.
Grewal and Rudolph publish a pure-state quantified upper bound for QMA(2), without a BQEXP containment.
Liu and Wu’s revised manuscript gives upper bounds for restricted stoquastic unentangled verification; it distinguishes that setting from general QMA(2).

sentences: The question asks whether every problem with two unentangled quantum proofs can be decided in quantum exponential time without proofs.
The verifier is polynomial-time and may process both proofs jointly, but the proofs must initially be a product state.
The deciding algorithm must be uniform and have bounded error on every promised input.
The standard upper bound uses nondeterministic exponential time, which does not give the requested algorithm.
Recent quantified and stoquastic results concern different upper-bound models and leave this inclusion unresolved.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem specifies yes-inputs \(Y\) and no-inputs \(N\); on inputs outside \(Y\cup N\), a deciding algorithm has no correctness requirement but must still obey its resource bound. A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\). A pure state on \(w\) qubits is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^w}\). Two unentangled proofs have the tensor-product form \(|\psi\rangle\otimes|\phi\rangle\), where each vector describes at most \(w(n)\) qubits for some polynomial \(w\). Arbitrary entanglement within either proof is allowed, but entanglement between the proofs is excluded.

Membership in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) means that one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, on input \(x\), generates a quantum circuit \(V_x\) of polynomial size. The circuit takes the two proof registers and zero-initialized work qubits, and finally measures an output bit. Write \(a_x(\psi,\phi)\) for its acceptance probability. Its guarantees are \[x\in Y\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\ge2/3,\qquad x\in N\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\le1/3.\] The two proofs are sent once; there is no later interaction. The same definition results if mixed product states or convex mixtures of product states are permitted, by linearity of acceptance probability. The verifier need not certify that an arbitrarily supplied entangled pair is a product: unentanglement is the proof model's assumption.

Use the fixed finite gate set consisting of Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT, acting on named wires. Circuit size counts every gate; every initialized or proof qubit counts toward the relevant qubit bound. Uniform generation outputs the full gate and wire list.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\) means that one deterministic circuit generator, on input \(x\) of length \(n\), runs in at most \(2^{p(n)}\) steps and outputs a circuit with at most \(2^{p(n)}\) gates and qubits, using the same finite gate set. The circuit begins with zero-initialized qubits, receives no proof or advice, and accepts yes-inputs with probability at least \(2/3\) and no-inputs with probability at most \(1/3\). Classical dependence on \(x\) is through the generator. Polynomial overheads in the generator and circuit can be absorbed into \(p\). No oracle or postselection is available. Probability in both models is ordinary quantum measurement probability.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. Inclusion requires a bounded-error, uniform exponential-time quantum decision procedure for every problem satisfying the stated two-proof verification definition. Separation requires a promise problem in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) with no such decision procedure. Simulations only for restricted verifiers, shorter proofs, or a different completeness-soundness gap do not suffice.

context_blocks.text: Classically, two existential witnesses can simply be concatenated. In this quantum model, allowing an arbitrary joint state would remove the product restriction and give the ordinary single-proof model. That restriction is therefore part of the computational resource, rather than an incidental communication detail.

A known upper bound is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\), where \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) allows nondeterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). Guessing sufficiently accurate classical descriptions of the two states and verifying them explains this bound. Enumerating all such descriptions is much more expensive, so this does not give a deterministic or quantum exponential-time algorithm.

The 2026 hierarchy result gives a structural upper bound using competing quantifiers over pure quantum states. Its stated containments still end at nondeterministic exponential time. An existential/universal characterization does not itself implement a bounded-error quantum decision procedure.

The July 2026 work obtains exponential-time algorithms for a stoquastic restriction, designed to remove destructive interference. Its verifier restrictions are substantive, so those algorithms do not yield the requested simulation for general quantum verifiers.

cards.title: Quantum query–space tradeoffs for collisions and distinctness
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the functions \(T_b(n,m,S)\) for \(b\in\{\mathrm{collision},\mathrm{distinctness}\}\): the minimum worst-case number of quantum queries needed by an algorithm with at most \(S\) qubits of total retained memory to solve the specified decision problem with error at most \(1/3\). The input is an oracle for \(f:[n]\to[m]\). In the collision problem, \(n\) is even and \(f\) is promised to be either injective or exactly two-to-one; distinguish these cases. In element distinctness there is no promise; decide whether \(f\) is injective. The full parameter domain is \(m\ge n\ge2\) and \(S\ge4(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil)+10\), with integer parameters. This card selects the source's total-memory tradeoff, allowing all retained memory to be quantum; separating classical and quantum memory budgets is a further variant.
cards.why: Quantum collision and distinctness algorithms gain speed while retaining substantial information about queried values. Their optimal time/space tradeoffs would quantify how much memory is necessary for those advantages and develop lower-bound methods for problems whose output contains only one bit.
cards.status_note: Open in the 2021 source. Checked on 2026-09-14: the February 2026 work concerns nested collision finding; the September 2026 preprint gives claimed search bounds under label symmetry and explicitly leaves removal of symmetry open. Neither checked statement settles the unrestricted, worst-case decision tradeoff formulated here. The total-memory convention is explicit.

progress.text: Aaronson lists the two query/space tradeoffs as open, distinguishing them from the already established unrestricted-query complexities.
Hao, Huang and Liu give space-sensitive lower bounds for nested collision finding, addressing a related short-output barrier.

Magniez and Zur post claimed tight search tradeoffs under label symmetry and explicitly retain the unrestricted-algorithm question. These are restricted-model progress, not a resolution of the displayed decision curves.

importance.reason: Characterizes simultaneous time and memory limits for basic quantum collision tasks, beyond query complexity alone.

sentences: The question asks for the optimal quantum query cost of collision testing and element distinctness at every allowed memory budget.
The oracle returns an output symbol, and the algorithm must decide the answer with bounded worst-case error.
All retained storage counts, including classical tables and query registers.
Recent lower bounds concern nested collision tasks or search algorithms restricted by label symmetry.
The target remains matching upper and lower bounds for unrestricted algorithms solving the two decision problems.

cards.definitions:
The notation \([r]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Injective means that distinct inputs have distinct outputs. Exactly two-to-one means that every value in the image has exactly two preimages; unused output values have none. The required output is one bit, not a pair of colliding indices.

Let \(a=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) and \(v=\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil\). A query maps \(|i,y,z\rangle\) to \(|i,y\mathbin{\oplus}\operatorname{enc}(f(i)),z\rangle\), with \(a\) address qubits, \(v\) answer qubits and a remaining work register. Here \(\operatorname{enc}\) is the length-\(v\) binary encoding and \(\oplus\) is bitwise addition modulo two. For address zero or an address larger than \(n\), use the all-zero answer. One call returns one entire output symbol and costs one query. The address and answer registers are included in \(S\).

An algorithm begins with an input-independent state on at most \(S\) qubits, alternates a fixed finite sequence of input-independent quantum channels with oracle calls, and ends with a two-outcome measurement. A density matrix describes its state. An allowed intervening channel has the form \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\), where the finitely many matrices satisfy \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\); it maps the retained memory back into the same bounded space. This allows measurement, randomization and resetting memory. Discarded information cannot be retrieved later. Any measurement outcomes, classical work bits, or tables that remain accessible must occupy the counted memory. Input-dependent classical control is therefore also stored in that memory. There is no external input-dependent advice, second oracle, or uncounted read/write storage.

The channels and measurement may depend on \(b,n,m,S\), but not on \(f\). Their descriptions and the input-independent instruction index are not workspace, and no uniformity, gate-count or computation-time restriction is imposed between queries. Arbitrary computation on the stored memory, including coherent access to stored tables, is free. All oracle calls count, including preprocessing and calls on branches later discarded. The finite query budget is worst-case, and correctness must hold on every valid oracle, with probability at least \(2/3\). The stated space floor allows elementary repeated scans, so both minima are finite; no upper limit on \(S\) is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply positive functions \(H_b(n,m,S)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(cH_b(n,m,S)\le T_b(n,m,S)\le CH_b(n,m,S)\) for both tasks throughout their parameter domains. Both algorithms and matching lower bounds must respect the stated memory budget; an unrecorded increase in space is not allowed. The functions must describe the asymptotic dependence on the parameters, not simply repeat the optimization defining \(T_b\). Bounds for collision search, random inputs, or label-symmetric algorithms alone do not establish the required worst-case decision tradeoffs.

context_blocks.text: Without a restrictive memory budget, the familiar quantum query scales are \(n^{1/3}\) for the collision promise and \(n^{2/3}\) for element distinctness in their standard parameter regimes. Their optimality as query bounds does not determine the memory needed to attain them.

A classical table that can be queried coherently still occupies memory in this formulation. Counting its bits prevents a large external table from making a small-qubit algorithm appear to use little total storage. The separate question of which part of the storage must preserve quantum coherence is not resolved by a total-space bound.

The February 2026 work establishes memory lower bounds for a nested collision task with short output. Its input uses an additional oracle and a different success condition, so its lower bounds are not automatically the tradeoffs for either decision problem defined here.

The September 2026 preprint claims tight bounds for collision search and element-distinctness search under a label-symmetry restriction. Its Section 1.4 explicitly leaves removal of that restriction open. Permuting labels to symmetrize an arbitrary algorithm may require additional memory, which prevents treating symmetry as free.

cards.title: Constant-round quantum refereed games versus \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{QRG}_{\mathrm{const}}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? For every promise problem \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) admitting a quantum refereed game with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, two competing provers and some fixed constant \(k\) of interaction cycles, must there be a deterministic algorithm deciding \(\Pi\) using polynomial space? For \(x\in Y\), a yes-prover must have a strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) against every no-prover strategy. For \(x\in N\), a no-prover must have a strategy that makes it reject with probability at least \(2/3\) against every yes-prover strategy. The constant \(k\) and the polynomial bounds may depend on the problem and verifier, but not on input length.
cards.why: These games combine efficient quantum verification with competition between two powerful provers who have different information. Locating constant-length games would clarify whether repeated alternation of private interaction can increase computational power beyond polynomial space, even when only a few exchanges are allowed.
cards.status_note: The July 2026 source asks the general constant-round question. The primary game definitions, polynomial-length EXP characterization and bounded-turn PSPACE results were checked on 2026-09-14, with a bounded later-work search. The one-switch/DQIP result does not settle arbitrary constant interleaving, and no full resolution was identified.

progress.text: Gutoski and Watrous establish the competing-prover model and short quantum games, emphasizing private messages and interaction order.
Gutoski and Watrous characterize polynomial-length quantum refereed games by EXP.
Gutoski and Wu prove DQIP = QRG(2) = PSPACE for their specified one-switch interaction pattern and leave more general bounded-turn games outside that characterization.
The source problem list reiterates the question for a general constant number of rounds.

sentences: A quantum refereed game has two competing provers trying to make an efficient verifier accept or reject.
The provers exchange private quantum messages with the verifier and may keep private memory.
The question asks whether every game with a constant number of interaction cycles can be simulated in deterministic polynomial space.
Polynomial-space simulations are known for specific patterns in which interaction switches from one prover to the other only once.
Polynomially many general rounds capture exponential time, leaving the full constant-round boundary open.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem is a pair of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\); no answer is prescribed outside their union. Both provers know the classical input \(x\) and the verifier's complete specification. The yes-prover seeks acceptance and the no-prover seeks rejection. They cannot communicate directly and do not initially share an entangled state or correlated private randomness. Each may retain private quantum memory throughout the interaction, use randomness, and perform arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum operations without a time or memory bound.

The verifier is generated from \(x\), of length \(n\), by one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. Its total gate count, workspace, and total communicated qubits are polynomial in \(n\). It starts with zero-initialized registers. In each of at most \(k\) cycles, it applies a quantum circuit, sends one message register privately to each prover, and receives both response registers. Each prover acts only on its current message and its own retained private memory. The verifier then proceeds to the next cycle or its final two-outcome measurement. Messages to the two provers may be entangled through the verifier's preparation; this is part of the specified protocol. Empty messages are allowed. Sequential exchanges can be scheduled in separate cycles, so allowing every fixed \(k\) includes any constant-length message pattern. The verifier never gives a prover access to the other prover's private channel unless its own prescribed operations deliberately convey information from it.

Use a fixed universal finite gate set: Hadamard maps \(|0\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \(|1\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\); \(T\) multiplies \(|1\rangle\) by \(e^{i\pi/4}\) and fixes \(|0\rangle\); include \(T^{-1}\) and controlled NOT. The verifier's measurements, randomness and adaptive choices may be implemented coherently with polynomially many ancillary qubits. Prover operations are unrestricted quantum channels, expressible as \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\) with \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\), on their message and private registers. Initial private states can be prepared by those channels. All winning probabilities are over the resulting quantum measurement outcomes and private randomization. Each winning strategy may depend on \(x\), but must work against every opposing strategy on that input.

The class \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists here of promise problems decided by a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape and at most \(C(n+1)^r\) work-tape cells for fixed constants \(C,r\). It must halt on all inputs and give the correct answer on \(Y\cup N\). It has no oracle or advice. The simulator need only decide which side can force a win; it need not output either prover's strategy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. An inclusion proof must cover every fixed constant number of interaction cycles and every polynomial-time uniform verifier in the stated private-message model. A negative proof must exhibit a promise problem in this class with no deterministic polynomial-space decision algorithm. An exponential-time simulation, or a polynomial-space simulation only for one exchange pattern, does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: The winning-strategy requirements contain opposite quantifier orders on yes- and no-inputs. A prover must force its preferred outcome against all opposing strategies. This is different from two cooperating proof providers or a verifier receiving two unentangled existential witnesses.

Gutoski and Wu prove a polynomial-space simulation when all interaction with one prover is completed before interaction with the other begins. This includes their class QRG(2). Their result does not cover arbitrary repeated interleaving of the two private conversations.

Different papers count individual messages, turns and full send/receive rounds differently. This card fixes a complete interaction cycle explicitly. Since it asks about every constant cycle count, a constant change of counting convention does not change its scope.

With polynomially many messages, quantum refereed games capture \(\mathrm{EXP}\), deterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). This gives an upper bound for constant-length games, but it does not supply a polynomial-space simulation. The constant-length question remains meaningful even for classical messages.

cards.title: Black-box unitary synthesis
cards.formal: Is there one polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum oracle circuits \(\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\)-qubit unitary matrix \(U\), some Boolean function \(f_U:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to\{0,1\}\) makes the channel implemented by \(A_n^{f_U}\) approximate \(\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger\) within diamond distance \(1/10\)? The oracle input length \(m(n)\), total number of qubits, number of ordinary gates, and number of oracle calls must all be bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). The circuit family is chosen before \(U\); only the Boolean oracle may depend on \(U\). This is the fixed-constant-error version of black-box unitary synthesis.
cards.why: The question asks whether implementing arbitrary quantum transformations can be reduced efficiently to evaluating Boolean functions. A negative answer would establish a black-box obstruction to explaining all quantum transformation complexity through classical function computation, a central issue for unitary complexity and quantum cryptography.
cards.status_note: The source question is retained in Rosenthal’s May 2026 revision and the July 2026 Dong–Lombardi–Ma paper. Checked on 2026-09-14. Their bounds concern exponential-time upper bounds or restricted-query lower bounds, not a resolution of the displayed general polynomial-time, constant-diamond-error formulation.

Dong, Lombardi and Ma give additional one-query separations and approximation results for structured unitaries; the general polynomial-query question remains outside their claimed resolution.

importance.reason: A basic quantum transformation problem under black-box access, clarifying what an oracle interface permits.

sentences: The problem asks whether every quantum unitary can be implemented efficiently using an appropriately chosen Boolean oracle.
One fixed circuit family must work for all unitaries, with the desired unitary encoded only in the oracle.
The implementation must work on arbitrary inputs, including states entangled with an untouched reference.
Both total computation and coherent oracle access must remain polynomial in the number of input qubits.
Known exponential-time implementations and restricted-query lower bounds leave the general question unresolved.

cards.definitions:
An \(n\)-qubit system has state space \(\mathbb C^{2^n}\). A unitary matrix satisfies \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. A density matrix is a positive semidefinite matrix with trace one and describes a possibly mixed quantum state.

Each circuit receives an arbitrary \(n\)-qubit input, initializes all additional qubits to zero, and outputs a specified \(n\)-qubit register. Other registers are discarded, inducing a quantum channel \(\Phi_{A_n^{f_U}}\). The ordinary gate set is Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT. Gates may act on any named wires. One oracle call applies \(|z,b\rangle\mapsto|z,b\mathbin{\oplus}f_U(z)\rangle\) to the address and answer registers, including on superpositions; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. All calls use the same fixed Boolean function. Oracle inputs and answer registers count toward the qubit bound. The oracle's own computation is uncharged, but every ordinary gate and each oracle call counts toward circuit size. General adaptive quantum computation is allowed through its equivalent coherent circuit representation with polynomially many ancillas.

Uniformity means that a single deterministic Turing machine, on input \(1^n\), outputs the complete gate and wire list in time polynomial in \(n\). It receives no description of \(U\). The oracle function may be arbitrary, and no efficient procedure for computing it or deriving it from \(U\) is required. No additional quantum advice, input-dependent initial ancilla, postselection, or other oracle is available.

For channels with \(n\)-qubit input and output, define their diamond distance by \[D_\diamond(\Phi,\Psi)=\tfrac12\sup_{\rho}\|((\Phi-\Psi)\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\rho)\|_1,\] where \(R\) is an untouched \(n\)-qubit reference register and the supremum ranges over density matrices on input and reference together. The trace norm is \(\|M\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{M^\dagger M}\). The desired inequality holds for every input, including one entangled with the reference. The constant \(1/10\) is the allowed channel-approximation error, not an acceptance-probability or heralded-success condition. Global phases of \(U\) are irrelevant to its channel.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a universal efficient oracle-circuit family exists, or a proof of its negation. A positive proof must supply the uniform circuit family and show the existence of a suitable Boolean oracle for every unitary while meeting all resource and diamond-distance bounds. A negative proof must rule out polynomially many sequential oracle calls with polynomial total computation. A lower bound restricted to one query, parallel queries, or a prescribed oracle encoding does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: Preparing a chosen state starts from a known blank input. Unitary synthesis must act correctly on an unknown state and preserve its coherent relationships with any external system. Preparing each output column of a matrix separately does not by itself implement the unitary on an arbitrary superposition.

The Boolean oracle is allowed to encode the desired transformation without a computational restriction. The difficulty lies in extracting and using that information through short coherent queries within polynomial total computation. Counting the number of possible ordinary circuits therefore does not alone refute this model.

Rosenthal gives an oracle implementation using time \(\widetilde O(2^{n/2})\), with exponentially small approximation error. This improves a more direct exponential construction but remains far above polynomial time. His matching lower bound is for a particular column-construction interface, not every possible Boolean oracle.

Lombardi, Ma and Wright rule out general one-query synthesis and the corresponding polynomial parallel-query setting with efficient resources. The July 2026 follow-up studies one-query separations for more structured unitary families. These results leave unrestricted polynomially many sequential queries as a different question.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
